trial_name: PneumA — Comparison of 8 vs 15 Days of Antibiotic Therapy for Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia in Adults (2003)
citation: Chastre J, Wolff M, Fagon JY, Chevret S, Thomas F, Wermert D, et al; PneumA Trial Group. Comparison of 8 vs 15 days of antibiotic therapy for ventilator-associated pneumonia in adults: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2003 Nov 19;290(19):2588-98.
trial_type: RCT — multicenter, randomized, noninferiority, double-blind to day 8
one_liner: An 8-day antibiotic course for VAP was noninferior to 15 days for 28-day mortality and overall recurrence, but nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli had higher recurrence with shorter treatment.

pico.population: Adult ICU patients with bronchoscopically confirmed VAP receiving appropriate initial empirical antibiotic therapy.
pico.outcome: 28-day all-cause mortality and microbiologically documented recurrent pulmonary infection.

background.existing_knowledge: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) was historically treated with 14–21 days of antibiotics due to fear of relapse, especially with Gram-negative organisms.
background.knowledge_gap: Prolonged broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy increases resistance selection pressure and superinfections, but robust evidence supporting shorter duration was lacking.
background.hypothesis: An 8-day antibiotic course is noninferior to a 15-day course for 28-day mortality and recurrent pulmonary infection, while increasing antibiotic-free days and reducing resistant pathogen emergence.

methods.design: Multicenter, randomized, double-blind (until day 8), noninferiority trial conducted in 51 ICUs in France.
methods.setting: 51 adult ICUs in France; patients enrolled between study period with randomisation occurring 3 days post-bronchoscopy after microbiological confirmation.

inclusion: New and persistent infiltrate on chest radiography
Purulent tracheal secretions, temperature >= 38.3°C, or leukocyte count > 10,000/µL (>= 1 required for ARDS)
Positive quantitative cultures from BAL (>= 10^4 CFU/mL) or protected specimen brush/catheter (>= 10^3 CFU/mL)
Initiation within 24 hours of bronchoscopy of appropriate empirical antibiotics active against causative organism(s)
exclusion: Immunosuppressants or long-term corticosteroids (>= 0.5 mg/kg/day for > 1 month)
Extrapulmonary infection requiring > 8 days of therapy diagnosed between days 1–3
Early-onset pneumonia (< 5 days mechanical ventilation) without prior antibiotics in preceding 15 days

methods.intervention: Antibiotic therapy discontinued at end of day 8 unless needed for documented pulmonary recurrence or pre-existing infection. Initial broad-spectrum beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside or fluoroquinolone encouraged, with de-escalation at 48–72 hours.
methods.comparison: Antibiotic therapy continued to end of day 15 using same initial choice and de-escalation strategy.
methods.blinding: Allocation concealed via central interactive voice system; double-blind until day 8, at which point continuation vs cessation unblinded treatment group.
methods.sample_size_power: 400 patients (200/group) provided 90% power with alpha 10% to exclude a 10% noninferiority margin, assuming 15-day rates of 40% mortality and 25% recurrence; 4 planned interim analyses.
methods.primary_outcome: 28-day all-cause mortality and microbiologically documented recurrent pulmonary infection.
secondary_outcomes: Unfavourable outcome by day 28 (death, pulmonary recurrence, or new antibiotics > 48h)
Emergence of multiresistant pathogens among recurrences
methods.follow_up: Daily assessment to day 28 after bronchoscopy; vital status recorded at hospital discharge and day 60.

headline_bullets: 8-day therapy met noninferiority criteria for 28-day mortality (18.8% vs 17.2%) and overall pulmonary recurrence (28.9% vs 26.0%).
Short-course therapy significantly increased antibiotic-free days by 4.4 days (P < 0.001).
Nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli showed significantly higher recurrence with 8-day therapy (40.6% vs 25.4%).
Recurrent infections in the 15-day group had a higher rate of multiresistant pathogens (62.3% vs 42.1%, P = 0.04).

outcomes_table.note: Met 10% noninferiority margin; required quantitative bronchoscopic culture
Days 9–15 separation was 1.3 (2.3) vs 6.6 (1.4) days (MD -5.3, 90% CI -5.6 to -5.0)
Composite of death, recurrence, or new antibiotics > 48h
Higher diagnostic testing rate in 8-day group post-unblinding
Proportion of recurrences with multidrug-resistant pathogens

subgroup_table.subgroup: Nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli stratum (recurrence at day 28)

safety: No excess mortality observed with 8-day therapy at day 28 (18.8% vs 17.2%) or day 60 (25.4% vs 27.9%).
Multidrug-resistant pathogen emergence was higher among recurrent infections in the 15-day group (62.3% vs 42.1%, P = 0.04).

domains.notes: Central IVRS, stratified by center, block size 4; concealed allocation until day 8.
Double-blinded until day 8, after which unblinding occurred. Bronchoscopy rate for suspected recurrence was higher in the 8-day arm (60.9% vs 45.6%, P = 0.003), introducing detection bias.
402 randomized, 1 withdrew consent in 15-day group; 401 analyzed (197 vs 204) by intention-to-treat.
Clear exposure separation achieved (-4.5 treatment days). Subsequent post-regimen antibiotic courses occurred in 46.3% vs 44.3% of survivors.

Well matched for SAPS II (47 vs 47), SOFA (8 vs 8), septic shock (24.4% vs 21.1%); modest imbalance in male sex (76.6% vs 67.6%, P = 0.046). Day 3 randomization excluded 70 early deaths and 79 with inappropriate initial antibiotics.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate due to post-day 8 unblinding and differential bronchoscopy investigation rates, alongside delayed day-3 randomization.

domains.notes: Adult ICU patients in France with bronchoscopically confirmed VAP and confirmed appropriate initial empiric coverage; excludes immunocompromised patients and SAPS II > 65.
Requires quantitative bronchoscopic diagnostic protocols; generalizability is limited where VAP is diagnosed clinically or where early empiric antibiotic failure is common.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is moderate and applies best to ICU patients with bronchoscopically confirmed VAP receiving prompt appropriate initial antibiotics.

strengths: Multicenter design across 51 ICUs with rigorous microbiological confirmation using quantitative cultures.
Clear separation of antibiotic exposure with direct measurement of antibiotic-free days.
Prespecified microbiological subgroup analyses isolating nonfermenting Gram-negative pathogens.
limitations: Day 3 randomization enriches for survivors with early appropriate therapy, excluding early treatment failures.
Unblinding at day 8 led to significantly higher re-bronchoscopy rates in the 8-day group, introducing ascertainment bias for recurrence.
Permissive noninferiority margin of 10% and reliance on 90% confidence intervals for primary outcomes.
High rate of subsequent antibiotic use for extrapulmonary infections attenuated overall duration contrast.

critical_appraisal.summary: PneumA demonstrated that 8 days of antibiotics is effective and safe for most VAP cases, though unblinding and subgroup signals in nonfermenters require clinical nuance.
strengths: Microbiologically validated VAP diagnosis via quantitative bronchoscopic sampling
Demonstrated clear reduction in antibiotic exposure and lower rate of MDR recurrent pathogens
weaknesses: Ascertainment bias due to unblinded diagnostic re-investigation after day 8
Selection bias from delayed randomization at day 3 after excluding early non-responders

sections.authors_conclusion: In patients with microbiologically confirmed VAP receiving appropriate initial therapy, an 8-day course was noninferior to a 15-day course, reduced antibiotic exposure, and decreased resistant pathogen emergence, though recurrence was higher in nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Default to 7–8 days of antibiotic therapy for VAP when initial empirical therapy was appropriate and clinical response is good.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with microbiologically confirmed VAP who show clinical improvement on appropriate initial antibiotics.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean 8 days is sufficient for nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli (e.g., Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter) or patients with delayed clinical response, abscess, or empyema.
implementation_caveats: Assess response at day 8 before stopping therapy.
Consider extending therapy beyond 8 days for nonfermenting Gram-negative organisms or slow clinical response.
Requires reliable initial microbiological diagnostics and effective empiric antibiotic selection.

controversies.notes: By excluding 70 early deaths and 79 patients with inappropriate initial therapy prior to day 3, results apply only to patients who survived and received effective initial therapy.
A 10% absolute noninferiority margin for mortality and recurrence was criticized as overly broad.
Clinicians were unblinded at day 8 and performed significantly more re-look bronchoscopies in the 8-day arm (60.9% vs 45.6%), potentially over-detecting recurrence in the short-course arm.
Higher recurrence rate in nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli (40.6% vs 25.4%) led to guidelines recommending individualized longer treatment durations for these organisms.

unresolved_questions: What is the optimal duration for VAP caused specifically by Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Acinetobacter species?
Can biomarker-guided strategies (e.g., procalcitonin) safely shorten therapy below 8 days?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Treat VAP for 8 days rather than 15, but consider longer courses for nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli like Pseudomonas.
